passage: Come here, Norbu, let your grandmother Mola tell you about your cousins Ira and Pema. They fought like cats at home, over the remote, the window seat, everything. But last week I took them to the park in Gangtok. A big boy pushed Pema off the slide and called him a baby. Before I could stand up, Ira was there, hands on hips. "Don't you touch my brother!" And Pema, still sniffling, stood behind her and shouted, "Yeah! She's my sister!" The big boy walked off. On the way home they held hands. That night, they fought over the blanket again. I laughed. That is siblings, Norbu. They fight each other, and then they fight for each other.

qa.q: Where did Mola take Ira and Pema?
qa.a: She took them to the park in Gangtok.

qa.q: What does Pema shouting "She's my sister!" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows that despite their fights, he feels proud and loyal to Ira and wanted to stand with her.

qa.q: How could Mola or the parents build on the loyalty seen at the park?
qa.a: They could tell Ira and Pema what they noticed and praise them for standing up for each other, while still letting them sort out squabbles like the blanket fight themselves.

qa.q: What might the big boy have made of the two siblings standing together?
qa.a: He probably expected an easy target and did not count on a sister and brother standing up together, so he gave up and walked off.

grounding: It shows a grandparent seeing two quarrelling siblings defend each other against an outsider, showing that rivalry and loyalty live together.

passage: The Diwali fair was so crowded that Dadi could barely see over the heads, and she kept losing sight of Avni and Kashish near the rides. At home the two had fought all morning over who got the red lantern. Now Dadi spotted them by the merry-go-round. An older boy had cut in front of Kashish and shoved him. Avni stepped right between them. "Don't push my brother. He was here first." Kashish stood beside her, chin up. The older boy muttered and moved back. When Dadi finally reached them, they were climbing onto the same horse, laughing. Dadi smiled. The red lantern could wait.

qa.q: What had Avni and Kashish fought over that morning?
qa.a: They had fought over who got the red lantern.

qa.q: How can you tell Kashish felt braver with Avni beside him?
qa.a: He stood beside her with his chin up after she stepped between him and the older boy.

qa.q: What would you tell parents who worry about constant sibling fights?
qa.a: Fights are normal, and the same siblings can defend each other when it counts, so it helps to nurture that loyalty rather than only focusing on the quarrels.

qa.q: How does Dadi see the moment at the merry-go-round?
qa.a: She sees the loyalty beneath their rivalry and feels glad, smiling as they ride the same horse.

grounding: It illustrates a grandparent watching quarrelling siblings stand up for each other against an outsider, showing loyalty growing alongside rivalry.

passage:
Nana sat on the bench at the colony park in Lucknow, watching Neelam and her brother Kiku. They had fought all morning over the swing.

Then Thomas, a big boy from the next building, pushed Kiku off the slide. "Move, shorty."

Before Nana could get up, Neelam was there. She stood in front of Kiku, hands on hips. "Don't push my brother."

Thomas laughed. Kiku stood up beside her. "Yeah. Don't push my sister either."

Thomas shrugged and wandered off.

Nana watched them walk back to the swing, arguing again about whose turn it was. He smiled. The same two who fought at home had stood shoulder to shoulder in thirty seconds.

qa.q: What did Thomas say when he pushed Kiku?
qa.a: "Move, shorty."

qa.q: How does Nana feel watching Neelam and Kiku stand together?
qa.a: He feels warm and amused, smiling at how quickly they defended each other despite their fighting.

qa.q: What could Nana say to the children later?
qa.a: He could tell them he noticed how they stood up for each other, so they see the loyalty behind their fights.

qa.q: How might Kiku feel when Neelam steps in front of him?
qa.a: He probably feels protected and proud of his sister, and brave enough to stand beside her.

grounding: Nana notices his grandchildren, who fight constantly, defending each other against an outsider, showing rivalry and loyalty living together.

passage:
"Ganga Dadi, did you see that?"

"I saw, Indu. Tell me what happened."

"Ronit from 5B called Meenu a crybaby in front of everyone."

"And?"

"And I told him to shut up and say sorry."

"You? The girl who called Meenu a crybaby herself this morning?"

"That's different, Dadi. I'm her sister. I'm allowed."

"Ah."

"And then Meenu said to Ronit, 'Leave my didi alone, or I'll tell Sir.' She's only in Class 3!"

"So you defended her, and she defended you."

"...I guess."

"And now?"

"Now we're going home and we'll probably fight about the TV."

Dadi laughed. "That's how it will be all your lives."

qa.q: What did Ronit call Meenu?
qa.a: A crybaby.

qa.q: How does Ganga Dadi seem to feel listening to Indu?
qa.a: She seems amused and quietly pleased, seeing loyalty behind the sisters' rivalry.

qa.q: What does Dadi's last comment suggest about the sisters' bond?
qa.a: That fights and loyalty will live together all their lives, and the bond forged through fights can become lifelong support.

qa.q: How might Meenu feel after standing up for her didi?
qa.a: She probably feels brave and proud, even though she's only in Class 3.

grounding: Ganga Dadi hears how Indu and her younger sister, who tease each other, defended each other against a classmate, showing rivalry and loyalty together.

passage:
I'm Urmila, Jasleen and Gurnoor's Nani, and I've spent every summer watching those two fight. Over the window seat, the last mango, the remote. You name it.

But last week at the park, something happened. A group of older girls started laughing at Gurnoor's thick glasses. I was about to get up.

Jasleen got there first. She walked straight up to them and said, "That's my sister. Leave her alone." Then she took Gurnoor's hand and walked her away.

Ten minutes later, they were fighting again, about who got to sit on the higher swing.

I sat on my bench and laughed. That's siblings. They'll fight each other their whole lives, and fight for each other too.

qa.q: What were the older girls laughing at?
qa.a: Gurnoor's thick glasses.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel watching Jasleen defend Gurnoor?
qa.a: Urmila felt amused and touched, laughing at how quickly the sisters went from defending each other to fighting again.

qa.q: What does Urmila's story suggest about sibling fights?
qa.a: That rivalry and loyalty live side by side, and fighting siblings can still become each other's lifelong support.

qa.q: How might Gurnoor have felt when Jasleen took her hand?
qa.a: She probably felt protected and grateful, less hurt by the older girls.

grounding: Urmila, a grandmother, watches her granddaughters who always fight defend each other at the park, showing rivalry and loyalty together.

passage: Note for Ankita and Uday's parents, from Nana, Sunday. You asked me to write down how the week went while you were away, so here is one moment I don't want you to miss. Those two fought over the swing, the last paratha and the window seat nearly every day. But on Friday at the park, a bigger boy grabbed Uday's cricket bat and called him "shorty". Before I could even stand up, Ankita marched over and said, "Give it back. He's my brother." Uday stood right behind her, fists clenched. The boy handed the bat back. On the walk home they argued about who had been braver. I bought them both a kulfi and told them I was proud of how they stood together, not of any fighting. I think this is what you've been hoping to see.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy call Uday?
qa.a: He called him "shorty".

qa.q: How does Nana seem to feel about what happened at the park?
qa.a: Nana seems proud and moved, eager that the parents should not miss seeing the two stand together.

qa.q: What did Nana do on the walk home that encouraged the right lesson?
qa.a: Nana praised them for standing together rather than for any fighting, and treated them both to kulfi.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt when Ankita said, 'He's my brother'?
qa.a: Uday probably felt protected and proud, backing her up with clenched fists instead of feeling small.

grounding: Shows a grandparent noticing siblings who fight almost daily defending each other against an outsider, rivalry and loyalty living side by side.
